The act of waking, or the state of being awake; the state of not sleeping.
{{smaller block|<poem>Making such difference ’twixt ''wake'' and sleep

'''3.''' A row of damp green grass. ''Encyc. Dict.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''wakeful''' (wāk′fu̇l), ''a.'' [Early mod. E. ''wakefull''; < ''wake''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ful''; a late ME. form substituted for AS. ''wacol'', ''wacul'' (= L. ''vigil''), vigilant, wakeful.] '''1.''' Indisposed or unable to sleep; affected by insomnia.
{{smaller block|Two swains whom love kept ''wakeful'' and the Muse.
{{right|''Pope'', Spring, l. 18.}}
<poem>And her clear trump sings succor everywhere
By lonely bivouacs to the ''wakeful'' mind.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Commemoration Ode, ix.}}}}
'''2.''' Watchful; vigilant.
{{smaller block|<poem>Nor hundred eyes,
Nor brasen walls, nor many ''wakefull'' spyes.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. ix. 7.}}
<poem>Intermit no watch
Against a ''wakeful'' Foe. ''Milton'', P. L., ii. 463.</poem>}}
'''3.''' Rousing from, or as from, sleep.
{{smaller block|The ''wakeful'' trump of doom must thunder through the deep.
{{right|''Milton'', Nativity, l. 156.}}}}
='''Syn. 1''' and '''2.''' See ''watchful''.

'''wakefully''' (wāk′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' [< ''wakeful'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] In a wakeful manner; with watching or sleeplessness.

'''wakefulness''' (wāk′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' [< ''wakeful'' + ''-ness''.] The state or character of being wakeful; especially, indisposition or inability to sleep.
{{smaller block|A state of mental ''wakefulness'' is favourable to attention generally.
{{right|''J. Sully'', Outlines of Psychol., p. 88.}}}}

verbs, one strong, the other weak: (''a'') < ME. ''waken'' (pret. ''wok'', ''wook'', ''woc''; pl. ''woken''; pp. ''waken'', ''wakin''), < AS. *''wacan'' (pret. ''wōc'', pp. *''wacen''), arise, come to life, originate, be born, = Goth. ''wakan'' (pret. ''wōk''), wake. (''b'') < ME. ''waken'', ''wakien'' (pret. ''waked'', pp. ''waked''), < AS. ''wacian'' (pret. ''wacode'', pp. ''wacod'') = OS. ''wakōn'' = OFries. ''waka'' = D. MLG. ''waken'' = OHG. ''wachēn'', ''wahhēn'', MHG. G. ''wachen'' = Icel. ''vaka'' = Sw. ''vaka'' = Dan. ''vaage'', wake; cf. AS. ''weccan'', ''weccean'' (pret. ''wehte'') = OS. ''wekkian'' = D. ''wekken'' = OHG. ''wecchen'', MHG. G. ''wecken'' = Goth. *''wakjan'', in comp. ''uswakjan'', arouse, awake; akin to L. ''vigil'', wakeful, watchful, ''vigere'', flourish, etc.: see ''vigil''. Cf. ''watch'', ''wait'', from the same ult. source; cf. also ''waken'', ''awake'', ''awaken''.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To be awake; continue awake; refrain from sleeping.
{{smaller block|John the clerk, that ''waked'' hadde al nyght.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Reeve’s Tale, l. 564.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And, for my soul, I can not sleep a wink:
I nod in company, I ''wake'' at night.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Imit. of Horace, I. i. 13.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I could ''wake'' a winter night,
For the sake of somebody.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', My Heart is Sair.}}}}

'''2.''' To be excited or roused from sleep; cease to sleep; awake; be awakened: often followed by a redundant or intensive ''up''.
{{smaller block|Look you, my lady ’s asleep: she’ll ''wake'' presently.
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, iii. 1.}}}}

'''3.''' To keep watch; watch while others sleep; keep vigil; especially, to watch a night with a corpse. [Prov. Eng. and Irish.]
{{smaller block|<poem>And they ''woke'' ther al that nyȝt,
With many torches & candle lyȝt.</poem>
{{right|''King Horn'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 96.}}}}
{{smaller block|The people assembled on the vigil, or evening preceding the saint’s-day, and came, says an old author, “to churche with candellys burnyng, and would ''wake'', and come toward night to the church in their devocion,” agreeable to the requisition contained in one of the canons established by king Edgar, whereby those who came to the wake were ordered to pray devoutly.
{{right|''Strutt'', Sports and Pastimes, p. 469.}}}}

'''4.''' To be active; not to be quiescent.
{{smaller block|I sleep, but my heart ''waketh''.
{{right|Cant. v. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|To keep thy sharp woes ''waking''.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 1136.}}}}

'''5.''' To be excited from a torpid or inactive state, either physical or mental; be put in motion or action.
{{smaller block|<poem>Gentle airs, due at their hour,
To fan the earth now ''waked''. ''Milton'', P. L., x. 94.

Breathed in fitful whispers, as the wind
Sighs and then slumbers, ''wakes'' and sighs again.</poem>
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Sympathies.}}}}

'''6†.''' To hold a late revel; carouse late at night.
{{smaller block|<poem>The king doth ''wake'' to-night, and takes his rouse,
Keeps wassail, and the swaggering up-spring reels.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 4. 8.}}}}

'''7.''' To return to life; be aroused from the sleep of death; live.
{{smaller block|That, whether we ''wake'' or sleep, we should live together with him.
{{right|1 Thess. v. 10.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To rouse from sleep; awake; awaken: often followed by a redundant or intensive ''up''.
{{smaller block|She hath often dreamed of unhappiness and ''waked'' herself with laughing.
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, ii. 1. 361.}}}}
{{smaller block|She’s asleep with her eyes open; pretty little rogue; I’ll ''wake'' her and make her ashamed of it.
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, iii. 2.}}}}
'''2.''' To watch by night; keep vigil with or over; especially, to hold a wake over, as a corpse. See ''wake''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', 3.
{{smaller block|And who that wil ''wake'' that Sparhauk 7 dayes and 7 nyghtes, and, as sume men seyn, 3 dayes and 3 nyghtes, with outen Companye and with outen Sleep, that faire Lady schal zeven him, whan he hathe don, the first Wyssche that he wil wyssche of erthely thinges.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 145.}}}}
{{smaller block|You were right, dear, from first to last, concerning the poor cratur’s dead child: she did not want to have it ''waked'' at all, for she is not that way—not an Irishwoman at all.
{{right|''Miss Edgeworth'', Garry Owen.}}}}
'''3.''' To arouse; excite; put in motion or action: often with ''up''.
{{smaller block|Prepare war, ''wake up'' the mighty men. Joel iii. 9.
<poem>Thou hadst been better have been born a dog
Than answer my ''waked'' wrath!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iii. 3. 363.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>He felt as one who, ''waked up'' suddenly
To life’s delight, knows not of grief or care.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, II. 171.}}}}
'''4.''' To bring to life again, as if from the sleep of death; revive; reanimate.
{{smaller block|<poem>To second life
''Wak’d'' in the renovation of the just.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 65.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The willows, ''waked'' from winter’s death,
Give out a fragrance like thy breath.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', The Arctic Lover.}}}}
'''5.''' To disturb; break.
{{smaller block|<poem>No murmur ''waked'' the solemn still,
Save tinkling of a fountain rill.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., iii. 26.}}}}

'''wake'''<sup>1</sup> (wāk), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wake'', < AS. *''wacu'', wake or watch, in comp. ''niht-wacu'', a night-wake (= Icel. ''vaka'' = MLG. ''wake'', watch), < ''wacan'', wake: see ''wake''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'' Hence, in comp., ''likewake'', ''lichwake''.]   '''1†.''' The act of waking, or the state of being awake; the state of not sleeping.
{{smaller block|<poem>Making such difference ’twixt ''wake'' and sleep
As is the difference betwixt day and night.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., iii. 1. 219.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I have my desire, sir, to behold
That youth and shape which in my dreams and ''wakes''
I have so oft contemplated.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Staple of News, ii. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' The act of watching or keeping vigil, especially for a solemn or festive purpose; a vigil; specifically, an annual festival kept in commemoration of the completion and dedication of a parish church; hence, a merrymaking; a festive gathering. {{smaller|The wake was kept by an all-night watch in the church. Tents were erected in the churchyard to supply refreshments to the crowd on the following day, which was kept as a holiday. Through the large attendance from neighboring parishes at wakes, devotion and reverence gradually diminished, until they ultimately became mere fairs or markets, characterized by merry-making and often disgraced by indulgence and riot. In popular usage this word has the same meaning as ''vigil.'' The wake or revel of country parishes was, originally, the day of the week on which the church had been dedicated; afterward, the day of the year. In 1536 an act of convocation appointed that the wake should be held in every parish on the same day, namely, the first Sunday in October; but it was disregarded. Wakes are expressly mentioned in the “Book of Sports” of Charles I. among the feasts which should be observed. The wake appears to have been also held on the Sunday after the day of dedication; or, more usually, on the day of the saint to whom the church was dedicated. In Ireland it is called the ''patron day.''   ''Brand,'' Popular Antiquities.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>He is wit’s pedler, and retails his wares
At ''wakes'' and wassails, meetings, markets, fairs.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., v. ii. 318.}}}}
{{smaller block|Didsbury ''Wakes'' will be celebrated on the 8th, 9th, and 10th of August [1825]. . . . The enjoyments consist chiefly of ass-races, for purses of gold; prison-bar playing, and grinning through collars, for ale; . . . and balls each evening.
{{right|Quoted in ''Hone’s Year Book'', col. 958.}}}}

'''3.''' An all-night watch by the body of the dead, before burial. {{smaller|This custom seems to be of Celtic origin, and is now characteristic of Ireland, or of the Irish in other countries; but it was formerly observed in Scotland and Wales. It probably originated from a superstition that the body might be carried off by invisible spirits, or from a more rational fear of injury to it from wild beasts. In early literature it has the name of ''likewake, lichwake.'' The wake was originally a combination of mourning for the dead and rejoicing in his memory and for his deliverance, but in later times has often degenerated into a scene of wild grief and gross orgies. See ''likewake.''}}
{{smaller block|<poem>How that the ''liche-wake'' was y-holde
Al thilke night. ''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 2100.</poem>}}

{{smaller block|The ''late-wake'' is a ceremony used at funerals. The evening after the death of any person, the relations and friends of the deceased meet at the house, attended by a bagpipe or fiddle; the nearest of kin, be it wife, son, or daughter, opens a melancholy ball, dancing and greeting, i. e. crying violently, at the same time; and this continues till daylight, but with such gambols and frolics among the younger part of the company that the loss which occasioned them is often more than supplied by the consequences of that night. If the corpse remain unburied for two nights, the same rites are renewed.
{{right|''Pennant'', Tour in Scotland, p. 112.}}}}

'''wake'''<sup>2</sup> (wāk), ''n.''   [= D. ''wak'', an opening in ice, < Icel. ''vök'' (''vak''-), a hole. opening in the ice, = Sw. ''vak'' = Norw. ''vok'' = Dan. ''vaage'', an opening in ice; allied to Icel. ''vökr'', moist, ''vökva'', moisten, water, > Sc. ''wak'', moist, watery, = D. ''wak'', moist; < Teut. √ ''wak'', wet, = Indo-Eur. √ ''wag'', L. ''umere'', be moist, Gr. ὑγρός, moist: see ''humid'', ''humor'', ''hygro-'', etc. Cf. OF. ''ouage'', F. ''ouaiche'', ''houache'', wake, < E.]   '''1.''' The track left by a ship or other moving object in the water. {{smaller|A ship is said to ''follow in the wake'' of another when she follows in the same track, and to ''cross the wake'' of another when she crosses the course in which the other has passed.}}
{{smaller block|In the ''wake'' of the ship (as ’tis call’d), or the smoothness which the ship’s passing has made on the sea.
{{right|''Dampier'', Voyages (an. 1699). (''Richardson.'')}}}}
'''2.''' Hence, a track of any kind; a course of any nature that has already been followed by another thing or person.
{{smaller block|Twice or thrice . . . a water-cart went along by the Pyncheon-house, leaving a broad ''wake'' of moistened earth.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, xi.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thence we may go on, in the ''wake'' of so many travellers and conquerors, to those lands beyond the sea.
{{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Venice, p. 294.}}}}

{{smaller block|A torpedo could be sent so closely in the ''wake'' of another as to take instant advantage of the opening made in the netting.
{{right|''Daily Telegraph'', Sept. 25, 1886. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''3.''' A row of damp green grass.   ''Encyc. Dict.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''wakeful''' (wāk′fu̇l), ''a.''   [Early mod. E. ''wakefull''; < ''wake''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ful''; a late ME. form substituted for AS. ''wacol'', ''wacul'' (= L. ''vigil''), vigilant, wakeful.]   '''1.''' Indisposed or unable to sleep; affected by insomnia.
{{smaller block|Two swains whom love kept ''wakeful'' and the Muse.

'''3.''' Rousing from, or as from, sleep.
{{smaller block|The ''wakeful'' trump of doom must thunder through the deep.
{{right|''Milton'', Nativity, l. 156.}}}}
='''Syn. 1''' and '''2.''' See ''watchful''.

'''wakefully''' (wāk′fu̇l-i), ''adv.''   [< ''wakeful'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.]   In a wakeful manner; with watching or sleeplessness.

'''wakefulness''' (wāk′fu̇l-nes), ''n.''   [< ''wakeful'' + ''-ness''.]   The state or character of being wakeful; especially, indisposition or inability to sleep.
{{smaller block|A state of mental ''wakefulness'' is favourable to attention generally.

'''waken''' (wā′kn), ''v.''   [< ME. ''waknen'', ''wacknen'', ''wakenen'', < AS. ''wæcnan'', arise, be aroused, be born (= Icel. ''vakna'', become awake, = Sw. ''vakna'' = Dan. ''vaagne'' = Goth. ''ga-waknan'', awake), with pass. formative ''-n'', < *''wacan'', etc., wake: see ''wake''<sup>1</sup>, and cf. ''awaken''.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To wake; cease to sleep; be awakened: literally or figuratively.
{{smaller block|So that he bigan to ''wakne''. ''Havelok'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2164.
<poem>’Tis sweet in the green spring
To gaze upon the ''wakening'' fields around.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', Spring-Time.}}}}

'''2.''' To keep awake; refrain from sleeping; watch.
{{smaller block|<poem>The eyes of heaven that nightly ''waken''
To view the wonders of the glorious Maker.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Mad Lover, v.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Now sleeps the crimson petal, now the white; . . .
The fire-fly ''wakens; waken'' thou with me.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, vii.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To excite or rouse from sleep; awaken.
{{smaller block|May the winds blow till they have ''waken’d'' death.
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, ii. 1. 188.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Go, ''waken'' Eve;
Her also I with gentle dreams have calm’d.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xii. 594.}}}}

'''2.''' To excite to action or motion; rouse; stir up.
{{smaller block|Yff we ''wackon'' vp werre with weghes so fele.
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2274.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I’ll shape his sins like Furies, till I ''waken''
His evil angel, his sick conscience.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Maid’s Tragedy, v. 2.}}}}

'''3.''' To excite; produce; call forth.
{{smaller block|<poem>Venus now wakes, and ''wakens'' love.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 124.}}}}
<poem>They introduce
Their sacred song, and ''waken'' raptures high.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iii. 369.}}}}
